lines: Jordan Lee
+1 (555) 010-2468 | jordan.lee@example.com | example.com/code/jordan-lee
EDUCATION
Western State University | M.S. in Computer Engineering | Metro City, USA | Sep 2024 - Expected Jun 2026
Eastern Institute of Technology | B.S. in Electrical Engineering | Metro City, Country | Sep 2018 - Jun 2022
EXPERIENCE
Eastern Robotics Co. | Junior Software Engineer | Metro City, Country | Aug 2022 - Jul 2024
- Owned the diagnostics service's monitoring dashboards across two major releases and the on-call rotation that used them.
- Reduced p95 API latency from 420 ms to 180 ms by adding a request cache and batching sensor reads, with load tests that fail the build if p95 exceeds 200 ms.
- Maintained the CI pipeline for the perception team's model releases, adding automated regression checks that shortened release cycles from 2 weeks to 3 days.

- Migrated 30 robot-fleet services from cron jobs to an event queue while rewriting the shared logging library, onboarding two new hires and taking over the weekend on-call rotation, which removed the nightly backlogs that delayed morning dispatch.
Mobility Systems Company | Machine Learning Engineering Intern | Metro City, USA | Oct 2024 - May 2025

- Built a diagnostics triage branch for an industrial inspection system that screens 800+ sensor signals per case with ML-extracted features, cutting the pending-case backlog 68% in the eight weeks after launch.
- Raised diagnostic accuracy on 1,200 held-out cases from 71% to 79% by fine-tuning a domain adapter on validated tool-use trajectories with assistant-only loss masking.
- Cut p95 latency of single-request edge inference by 40% by serving the INT8 engine with dynamic batching.
- Using grouped tool-use rollouts, a composite reward over accuracy, citation validity and call count, and a GRPO loop with a frozen SFT reference, reduced end-to-end latency 5%.
- Stabilised GRPO training on sparse rewards by sampling a single rollout per prompt, so each update used exactly one scored trajectory.
- Documented the triage branch's abstention rules and escalation paths for the on-call reviewers, who adopted them as the team's runbook.
PROJECTS
Agent Runtime Suite | Owner | TypeScript, Multi-Agent Systems | Aug 2025 - Present
- Drove adoption of AI-first engineering practices across the platform, accelerating delivery and improving outcomes for downstream teams.
- Cut p95 tool-call latency from 900 ms to 600 ms, a 50% reduction, by caching tool results and reusing completed sub-agent answers.
- Raised the runtime's task-completion rate by 12% on the benchmark suite, from 71% to 83%, by retrying failed sub-agent calls with their partial context.
Research-Agent Evaluation Framework | Contributor | LLM Evaluation | Feb 2025 - Jul 2025
- Upstreamed 8 citation and faithfulness metrics to an open-source research-agent framework, where they now run in the default benchmark for every release.
- Showed the evaluator tracks injected degradation with a Kendall correlation of 0.89 across 400+ report-level trials that removed citations, sources and claims.
- Traced 3 structural pipeline defects in stability, sourcing and parameter handling to their modules with layered instrumentation; each was fixed upstream.
SKILLS
Programming: Python, TypeScript, Git
ML & Agents: PyTorch, LoRA, GRPO, agent evaluation, Kubernetes

items.says: Experience is not ordered newest first.
items.because: Eastern Robotics Co. appears above the more recent Mobility Systems Company entry, breaking the expected reverse-chronological scan.

items.says: The monitoring-dashboard and on-call work has no measurable operational result.
items.because: Ownership across two releases shows scope, not whether detection, response, or alert coverage improved.

items.says: “Owned” frames the work as a duty, and the dashboard–rotation relationship is awkwardly worded.
The strongest achievement is not the opening phrase of the entry.
items.because: Leading with a responsibility statement delays the clearest quantified technical outcome.

items.says: “Fail the build” is in the present tense inside a past-tense bullet.
“Maintained” delays the concrete CI change and its release-cycle result.
The backlog result lacks a before-and-after comparison.
items.because: The 30 services measure scope, not how consistently or materially the nightly backlog was reduced.

items.says: The morning-dispatch result is buried among unrelated responsibilities, and “which removed” has an unclear antecedent.
Fine-tuning details make the primary technical contribution hard to scan.
items.because: The technical density competes with the held-out-case accuracy result and obscures which method mattered most.

items.says: Dynamic batching cannot explain a 40% latency reduction for single-request inference.
items.because: Batching combines concurrent requests; a single request cannot benefit and may incur batch-formation delay.

items.says: The latency result gives only a relative change and uses a dense workload phrase.
items.because: Without baseline and final p95 values, the reader cannot judge response time, and the comparison scope is hard to identify.

items.says: The stated GRPO reward cannot directly support the claimed 5% latency reduction.
items.because: The reward has no latency signal, and fewer calls do not establish a latency reduction without separate measurement and a demonstrated relationship.

items.says: The bullet leads with three method details, burying the result and the candidate’s specific action.
items.because: A scanning reader reaches the outcome only after the methods and cannot tell which design choice the candidate owned.

items.says: “Reduced end-to-end latency 5%” lacks a baseline or comparison point.
items.because: The reader cannot tell the starting latency, final latency, or comparison condition.

items.says: Sampling one rollout per prompt does not stabilize standard GRPO training.
items.because: GRPO needs multiple rollouts per prompt to compare relative rewards; with one, updates may be high-variance or uninformative.

items.says: “Stabilised GRPO training” does not identify an observable training result.
items.because: The reader cannot tell what measurable change stability refers to.

items.says: “Sampling a single rollout per prompt” and “exactly one scored trajectory” repeat the same fact.
The runbook adoption statement does not show its scope or duration.
The AI-first adoption claim gives no specific practice, beneficiary, or measurable outcome.
items.because: Without a baseline, delta, reach, or concrete practice, it reads as general praise rather than evidence of platform value.

items.says: “AI-first engineering practices” does not identify the practices or platform change that enabled adoption.
items.because: The reader cannot distinguish tooling, workflow changes, testing practices, or another technical contribution.

items.says: The reduction from 900 ms to 600 ms is 33.3%, not 50%.
items.because: The 300 ms decrease divided by the original 900 ms equals 33.3%.

items.says: The change from 71% to 83% is 12 percentage points, not an unqualified 12% increase.
items.because: The relative increase is approximately 16.9%.

items.says: The strongest achievement is not the opening bullet of the entry.
items.because: Leading with the broader adoption claim delays the concrete benchmark result and technical intervention.

items.says: The metrics contribution shows adoption but not the evaluation capability added or how it was integrated.
items.because: The technical depth of the contribution remains unclear.

items.says: The Kendall correlation does not identify the two things being correlated.
items.because: The reader cannot tell what the evaluator scores were compared against, making the 0.89 result hard to interpret.

items.says: “Tracks injected degradation” does not explain how the evaluator was tested.
items.because: The perturbations are listed, but the evaluation or ranking procedure connecting severity to evaluator behavior is not.

items.says: “Injected degradation” is compressed jargon that slows interpretation.
The three defect categories are too broad to show what failed or where tracing led.
“Each was fixed upstream” gives no post-fix result.
“Layered instrumentation” does not quickly explain what the candidate did.
Kubernetes appears in ML & Agents without supporting experience or project evidence.
items.because: A recruiter may question whether the skill was used substantively.
